html:
The map's label for the foraging peoples of the deserts of western North America, the Great Basin, the Mojave and parts of the Sonoran Desert and northern Mexico, shown from 1500 BCE to 1500.

Water and food were scarce, so people lived in small family groups and moved in a yearly round:

  • pine nuts gathered in autumn and stored for winter;
  • grass seeds, mesquite pods and, further south, agave hearts roasted in pits;
  • rabbits caught in drives with long nets, plus deer, mountain sheep and even insects;
  • around lakes and marshes, fish, waterbirds and cattail.

Baskets did much of the work of pottery, for gathering, storing and even cooking. Archaeologists call this way of life the Desert Archaic.

In historic times most of the Great Basin was home to Numic-speaking peoples, the Northern Paiute, Southern Paiute and Shoshone. Some scholars think they spread across it only about 1,000 years ago, but this is debated.

To the south-east, farming peoples grew maize in the same dry land, among them the Hohokam with their irrigation canals, the Mogollon and the Ancestral Puebloans. Foragers and farmers traded and sometimes switched ways of life as rains came and went.
